title: Class and Object
intro: How a Java class is written and how objects live in memory: references, constructors, `this`, encapsulation, static vs instance, pass-by-value, Strings, garbage collection and composition. Most code-tracing questions come from this chapter.

cards.title: Anatomy of a class
cards.body:
A class has three kinds of members:
**Fields** (attributes or instance variables) hold the state and are usually `private`.
**Constructors** set up a new object. They have the class's name and **no return type**.
**Methods** are the behaviour, usually `public`.

In UML: `-` means private, `+` means public, and **underlined** means static.

cards.title: Creating an object with new
cards.body:
Creating an object takes two steps:
1. `Rectangle rect;` declares a **reference variable**. No object exists yet.
2. `rect = new Rectangle();` allocates the object on the **heap**, runs the constructor, and stores the object's **address** in `rect`.

You can do both at once: `Rectangle rect = new Rectangle();`.
A reference holds an **address**, not the object itself. A primitive (`int n = 5`) holds its value directly.

cards.title: Default values, null and NullPointerException
cards.body:
**Fields** you don't initialise get default values. Numbers become 0 or 0.0, booleans become false, and references become `null`. **Local variables** get no default, so the compiler rejects any read before assignment.

`null` means the reference points to no object. Sending a message through it, as in `bill.comeDown()`, throws a **NullPointerException** at run time.

cards.title: Aliasing vs copying
cards.body:
`rect2 = rect1;` copies the **reference**, not the object. Now **one object has two names** (an alias). A change made through either name shows up through both.

To get a real second object, you must call `new` again. The slides do this in `copyObjects()`, which returns `new Rectangle(width, height)`.

cards.title: Constructors: default, overloaded
cards.body:
If you write **no constructor**, Java supplies a **default constructor**: no arguments, and it does nothing (`public Rectangle() { }`).
As soon as you write **any** constructor, that free default **disappears**. After that, `new Rectangle()` compiles only if you wrote a no-arg constructor yourself.

You can write several constructors with different parameter lists. This is **overloading**, and Java picks the one that matches the arguments.

  D -->|No| F[new Rectangle with no args: COMPILE ERROR]
keypoints: No constructors written: Java gives a no-arg default
Write one and the default disappears
Overloading = same name, different parameter lists

cards.title: this, and calling one constructor from another
cards.body:
`this` is the reference to the **receiver object**, the one the method was called on. In `rect1.findArea()`, `this` is `rect1`.

Use it when a parameter **shadows** a field: `this.width = width;`. Writing only `width = width;` assigns the parameter to itself, and the field stays 0.0.

`this(...)` calls **another constructor** of the same class. It must be the **first statement**.

cards.title: Encapsulation: private fields, get/set methods
cards.body:
Make the fields `private`, and let other classes reach them only through public **accessors** (get methods) and **mutators** (set methods). A mutator can **check values** to keep the data consistent, for example by capping the width at `MAX_WIDTH`.

If another class writes `r.width = -5;` while `width` is private, you get a **compile error**.

cards.title: static variables: one shared box
cards.body:
A **static** variable (a **class variable**) belongs to the **class**, not to any one object. There is **exactly one copy**, and every object shares it.
A field without `static` is an **instance variable**, and **every object gets its own copy**.

The slides use a static field to count how many Rectangles have been created: each constructor does `numRectangles++`.

cards.title: static methods and class constants
cards.body:
A **static method** (class method) runs **without an object**, so it has **no `this`**. That means it **cannot use instance fields or instance methods** directly. Call `findArea()` inside a static method and you get a compile error, and so does calling an instance method straight from `main`.
Call static methods **through the class name**: `Rectangle.getNumRectangles()`, `Math.sqrt(2)`.

A **class constant** is `public static final double MAX_WIDTH = 100;`: one copy, which cannot change, named in UPPER_CASE.

cards.title: Pass-by-value: copying a reference
cards.body:
Java **always** passes arguments **by value**. The method gets a **copy**.
**Primitive:** changing the copy (`n = 99`) does not change the caller's variable.
**Reference:** the copy points to the **same object**, so `r.setWidth(9)` is visible to the caller. Re-pointing the copy (`r = new ...`) affects only the method's own variable.

cards.title: String: an immutable object
cards.body:
`String` is a **class**, so a String variable holds a reference. Strings are **immutable**: methods such as `toUpperCase()` or `concat()` **return a new String** and leave the original unchanged.

`==` checks whether two references point to the **same object**. `equals()` checks whether the **characters are the same**. Always use `equals()` to compare text. Identical literals usually share one object, but `new String(...)` always makes a new one.

cards.title: Garbage collection: when is an object eligible?
cards.body:
Java has no destructor that you call yourself. The **garbage collector** frees objects automatically. An object becomes **eligible** once **no live reference can reach it**, for example when every variable that pointed to it has been set to `null` or re-pointed elsewhere. When the collector actually runs is not up to you.

The slides mention the `finalize()` method as Java's counterpart to a destructor. (Real Java deprecated `finalize()` in Java 9, so do not rely on it.)

cards.title: Object composition: objects inside objects
cards.body: An object can hold **references to other objects** as its fields. This is **object composition**, a **"has-a"** relationship: a Student has a Course. The field `private Course course;` stores an address. The Course object lives separately on the heap. You can also hold many objects in an array: `private Course[] course = new Course[3];`.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body:
**1.** Thinking `b = a` copies the object. It copies the reference only.
**2.** Expecting `new Rectangle()` to compile after you have written only a 2-argument constructor.
**3.** Writing `width = width;` in a constructor without `this.`.
**4.** Calling an instance method (or using `this`) inside `static main` without an object.
**5.** Thinking each object has its own copy of a static field.
**6.** Calling `s.toUpperCase();` and expecting `s` to change.
**7.** Comparing Strings with `==`.
**8.** Thinking an object is eligible for GC while another alias still points to it.
keypoints: References are addresses; = copies addresses
static has no this
Strings are immutable; use equals()
